A plover is a type of bird — specifically, a small to medium-sized shorebird found on nearly every continent on Earth.
What Kind of Bird Is It?

Plovers belong to a broad group called wading birds or shorebirds — birds that typically live near water, mud, sand, or open ground rather than in forests or trees. But plovers are actually more versatile than most shorebirds; while many of them do live near coastlines, lakes, and wetlands, some species are perfectly comfortable in dry grasslands, open fields, and even semi-desert landscapes. They are ground-dwellers — they spend almost all of their time on the ground, not perching in trees.
What Does a Plover Look Like?

Plovers are compact, rounded birds — think of a bird that looks a little stocky and well-built, not long and slender. Their legs are fairly long in proportion to their body, which suits their habit of running. Their bills are short and straight, often slightly swollen or bulbous at the tip — this is one of the easiest ways to tell a plover apart from other shorebirds like sandpipers, which have long, probing beaks.

One of the most recognizable features of plovers is their bold, striking markings. Many species have crisp bands of color — a dark ring around the neck, a black band across the chest, a white collar, or patches of black and gold on the head and back. These patterns make them look almost as if they're wearing little uniforms. The golden plover, for instance, is spangled with beautiful gold and black spots across its back. The killdeer, common in North America, wears two distinct black bands across its white chest.

Plovers have a very distinctive and charming way of finding food, and it's one of the things that sets them apart from other shorebirds. Instead of probing the mud or sand with a long bill (the way sandpipers do), plovers hunt by sight. They use a classic stop-and-go technique:

  1. They run forward in a quick burst.
  2. They stop suddenly and stand perfectly still, scanning the ground.
  3. They dart their bill down to snatch something they've spotted.
  4. Then they run again.

Watch a plover for even a minute, and this jerky, run-stop-peck pattern becomes impossible to miss. They eat insects, earthworms, small crustaceans, beetles, and other small invertebrates.

Plovers are found all over the world — from the Arctic tundra to tropical coastlines, from the grasslands of Africa to the beaches of Australia. Different species have adapted to very different environments. What they almost all share, though, is a preference for open spaces with clear sightlines — they're not forest birds. They need to see predators coming and need open ground to run.

Many plovers are migratory, traveling enormous distances between their breeding grounds and their wintering grounds. The American golden plover, for example, breeds in the Arctic and flies all the way to southern South America for the winter — one of the longest migrations of any bird.

Plovers are ground-nesters — they lay their eggs directly on the ground, usually in a shallow scrape in sand, gravel, or soil. Their eggs are typically camouflaged to blend into the surroundings, making them very hard to spot.

Because their eggs and chicks are so vulnerable on the ground, plovers have developed a remarkable defense strategy. When a predator gets too close to the nest, the parent plover will run away from the nest while dragging one wing along the ground and calling out — pretending to be injured. The predator, fooled into thinking it has spotted easy prey, follows the "wounded" bird. Once the parent has led the predator far enough away, it simply flies off, leaving the confused predator far from the nest. This behavior is called a distraction display or broken-wing display, and it is one of the most well-known examples of clever instinctive behavior in birds.

• Killdeer — the most familiar plover in North America, often found far from water, even in parking lots and lawns. Named for its piercing call that sounds like kill-dee.
  • Golden plovers — the American and European golden plovers, celebrated for their stunning plumage and extraordinary long-distance migrations.
  • Lapwing (also called the green plover or peewit) — common across Europe and Asia, known for its crested head and tumbling, acrobatic flight.
  • Ringed plover — a small, neat bird with a clean black-and-white face and a single dark breast band, very common on European coastlines.
  • Dotterel — a mountain and tundra plover, unusual because in this species the female is more brightly colored than the male (the reverse of what's typical in birds).

You'll encounter "plover" most often in the context of bird-watching, wildlife, and nature. It's a specific, precise word — not a vague, general term. When someone says "plover," they mean this particular group of ground-running, short-billed, boldly-patterned shorebirds with the characteristic run-stop-peck feeding style. If you see a compact bird sprinting across a beach or mudflat, stopping abruptly, then stabbing the ground with a short bill — chances are, you're looking at a plover.
